comparison: Perfect agreement on spatiotemporal findings (C61-C63, C93-C95, C97). Both evaluations support these claims as novel contributions showing regional and temporal specificity of SO-SP coupling, with peer reviewers explicitly affirming the frontal fast spindle findings align with theoretical predictions.

Complete agreement on null findings for sleep stage and bout moderators (C103-C105). Both evaluations accept these results without challenge, acknowledging the authors' note that findings are 'somewhat surprising' but treating them as valid.

Significant disagreement on interpretation of primary findings (C4, C53, C82, C114, C115). OpenEval finds claims supported with appropriate qualifications, while peer reviewers express uncertainty about practical significance despite statistical support, with one reviewer explicitly disagreeing that small effect sizes (~0.5% variance) justify calling coupling a 'general physiological mechanism.' OpenEval includes C87 which peer R1 also addresses.

Strong agreement on moderator analyses (C5, C55, C83, C101, C118). Both evaluations support these findings as key contributions. OpenEval notes some uncertainty about developmental effects due to limited studies, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm the moderator findings including age, spindle type, and channel location effects.

Agreement on methodological limitations in the literature (C109-C111). Both evaluations accept these observational findings about reporting practices and transparency issues. Peer reviewers implicitly acknowledge these concerns through comments about Bayesian methods being 'less transparent.'

Agreement on memory type moderation findings (C98-C99). Both evaluations support these claims. OpenEval notes limited sample sizes require cautious interpretation, while peer reviewers accept memory type as a key moderator without expressing concerns about the differential phase vs. strength predictions.

Strong disagreement on main conclusions (C6, C119). OpenEval finds conclusions supported by consistent evidence across analyses, noting small effect sizes as a caveat. Peer reviewers explicitly challenge the 'general physiological mechanism' conclusion, stating effect sizes are too small (< 0.10) to support such broad claims.

Partial agreement on SP amplitude findings (C85-C86, C116). Both evaluations support the findings about variability and specificity. However, peer reviewers express confusion about including amplitude measures since they don't directly measure coupling, though they don't challenge the results themselves.

Agreement on publication bias assessment (C90). Both evaluations accept the finding of no publication bias. OpenEval treats this as supporting robustness of results, and peer reviewers accept it without challenge as validating the effect size estimates.

Both address small effect sizes (C117). OpenEval treats this as an appropriate limitation acknowledgment common in neuroscience meta-analyses. Peer reviewers (R2) incorporate this concern more critically, using it to question whether effects support broad mechanistic conclusions.

OpenEval evaluates descriptive statistics about the meta-analysis dataset (C3, C48-C52) as straightforward data summaries. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these basic dataset characteristics.

OpenEval evaluates descriptive statistics for coupling measures (C75-C76, C79-C80) as straightforward data summaries with appropriate credible intervals. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these descriptive claims.

OpenEval evaluates findings on SP frequency and timing (C106-C107) as supported by data and citations, addressing literature confusion about SP classification. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these methodological clarifications.

OpenEval evaluates extensive background and prior research claims (C1-C47, C91-C92, C96, C102, C113) as appropriately cited and establishing theoretical framework. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.
